extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, logic, and methodology; scholars examining inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and improving inductive inferences: distinguishing kinds of induction, evidential standards, the special role of the law of causation, and limits on generalization and methods appropriate to coexistence vs succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief is not proof / standard of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief is not proof, and does not dispense with the necessity of proof. Evidence is not anything that produces belief but that which the mind ought to yield to, namely that by yielding to which belief is kept conformable to fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take the mere prevalence or instinctiveness of a belief as evidence. Appeal from one human faculty (judging) to those that take cognizance of fact (sense and consciousness). Distinguish causal psychological causes of belief (association, instinct) from legitimate evidence that makes belief conformable to fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid petitio principii in inductive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive methods often assume the universality of the law of causation; using that assumed universality to prove the law itself is circular (a petitio principii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not justify the law of universal causation by arguments that presuppose it. Claims that universality is 'instinctively' believed do not substitute for external evidence; one must seek evidence grounded in observation rather than mere mental disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limitations of induction per enumerationem simplicem
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple enumeration (generalization from observed instances without applying more elaborate methods) is fallible but can give some assurance suitable for ordinary conduct; its trustworthiness varies by case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a scale of trustworthiness: some generalizations (e.g., 'Food nourishes') are practically reliable despite originating in simple enumeration. Use scientific methods to improve and correct such inartificial generalizations where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific induction improves by resolving generalizations into broader laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement consists in correcting an inartificial generalization by showing it follows from, or conflicts with, a stronger induction—a generalization resting on a broader foundation of experience (e.g., the law of causation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test a generalization by attempting to deduce it from larger, better-established inductions or by showing that its falsity would contradict such broader laws. Employ the Four Methods where applicable to raise the degree of assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness increases with breadth of the generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The precariousness of simple enumeration is inversely proportional to the largeness of the generalization: as the subject-matter widens, simple enumeration becomes less liable to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad, widely diffused generalizations that hold everywhere within the range of possible observation are more secure than narrow, special generalizations which may depend on local collocations or absent counteracting agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical confirmation / falsification criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode of concluding from experience should be pronounced untrustworthy when subsequent experience refuses to confirm it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continued empirical testing: if later observations contradict a generalization, the method that produced it is unreliable. Prefer generalizations that survive new and broader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causation as foundational inductive axiom (within experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that everything which begins to exist must have some cause is the basis for the Methods of Induction applicable to sequences (successions) of phenomena; it can impart certainty to subordinate inductive propositions within the range of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, connect narrower inductions to the law of causation to increase their certainty. Treat the law of causation as a high-order induction justified by its extensive confirmation within observed phenomena, but recognize its justification is empirical and tied to observed domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit claims to the range of observation; avoid unwarranted extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities (including the law of causation) should be received as laws of that portion of the universe within the range of our means of sure observation, with only reasonable extension to adjacent cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confidently extend inductive generalizations to domains entirely beyond our experience (e.g., distant stellar regions) without evidence. Acknowledge that extrapolation beyond observed conditions is a supposition lacking empirical grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish uniformities of succession from uniformities of coexistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of succession (temporal sequences) fall under causation and admit Methods of Induction (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations). Uniformities of coexistence (properties that accompany kinds) are different and lack an analogous axiom enabling elimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply elimination-style methods (Method of Agreement or Difference, Concomitant Variations) naively to questions about coexistent properties. Recognize that for coexistence there may be no invariable coexistent to eliminate; different methodological tools are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify properties of kinds as ultimate or derivative before treating generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: A generalization about coexistence (e.g., 'All crows are black') may assert an ultimate property of a Kind or be a derivative empirical law depending on causes; one cannot be certain a property is ultimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing generalizations about kinds, investigate whether the coexistent property is caused (derivative) or truly an ultimate property of the kind. If derivative, treat the generalization as an empirical law subject to inductive testing; chemical and organized compounds often have properties traceable to causes, whereas only elementary substances yield confidently ultimate properties.
